analysis.one_liner: Approves the Keystone XL oil pipeline by act of Congress, bypassing remaining environmental review.
analysis.headline: The Senate voted 59–41 to approve the Keystone XL pipeline, but the vote had been set up to require 60 votes, so the bill failed by one.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have used an act of Congress to directly approve TransCanada's Keystone XL pipeline, which carries oil from Canadian tar sands to refineries on the Gulf Coast. It would have declared the State Department's January 2014 environmental review to fully satisfy every environmental law that normally applies — including the National Environmental Policy Act and Endangered Species Act review — and would have sent any legal challenge straight to a single appeals court in Washington. The bill never became law: on November 18, 2014, the Senate voted 59–41, one vote short of the 60 that the agreement setting up the vote required.
analysis.who_benefits: TransCanada, the company building the pipeline, gains a congressional green light without waiting for the normal presidential permitting decision or defending it in court. Canadian tar sands oil producers gain a new export route to Gulf refineries, and pipeline construction contractors gain a large temporary construction project. Supporters also pointed to construction jobs, though most are temporary; permanent pipeline operating jobs number in the dozens.
analysis.who_benefits_short: TransCanada and Canadian tar sands producers

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes TransCanada to build, connect, operate, and maintain the Keystone XL pipeline and its cross-border facilities, as described in its 2012 application to the State Department.

Declares the State Department's January 2014 Final Supplemental Environmental Impact Statement to fully satisfy the National Environmental Policy Act and any other law requiring federal agency consultation or review, including Endangered Species Act consultation, removing the remaining environmental checkpoints.
Keeps any federal permits already issued in effect and restricts legal challenges to a direct appeal to the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, shortening the legal path for the project.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people along the pipeline route and nationwide bear the risks: potential oil spills over aquifers and farmland, and the climate impact of enabling tar sands production, with the normal environmental review and court challenge processes waived. The federal government's usual permitting role is set aside for this one company.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities along the route and the public

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides the normal environmental process: it declares one environmental review sufficient under all applicable laws, including Endangered Species Act consultation, so no further federal agency review could be required.
It limits court challenges to a single direct appeal in the D.C. Circuit, cutting off the usual layered judicial review for a federal agency action of this size.
It is legislation naming and approving one company's specific project — TransCanada's 2012 application — rather than setting a general rule, so the benefits go to a single firm.

The pipeline would carry oil from Canadian tar sands, an especially carbon-intensive source, and its route crosses sensitive aquifer and ranchland in Nebraska and other states; a good-faith supporter would acknowledge these risks even while supporting the jobs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — temporary construction jobs and a convenient route for tar sands oil — is concentrated on one company and its suppliers. The costs are diffuse and long-lasting: waived environmental review, a shortcut around the courts, and the risk of spills and added carbon emissions. The bill stacks the process in the company's favor, which is the main reason critics fought it.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate took a direct vote, but the agreement that allowed the vote required 60 votes to pass, and it got only 59, so it failed by one vote and never went further in the 113th Congress.

narrative.text: Sen. John Hoeven introduced the bill on May 1, 2014 with 55 cosponsors — 44 Republicans and 11 Democrats — and it was placed on the Senate calendar two days later.
On November 18, 2014, the bill was laid before the Senate by unanimous consent under an order set on November 12, and failed passage 59–41, not reaching the 60 affirmative votes required.
Every one of the 45 Republicans voting voted yes; 14 of 53 Democrats voted yes and 39 voted no, and both independents voted no.
The bill provides that challenges to federal actions on the pipeline go only to the D.C. Circuit on direct appeal, and deems the 2014 environmental review sufficient under all environmental laws.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The normal permitting and court-review process survived, so landowners along the route and environmental and climate advocates are better off than under the bill. TransCanada did not get the congressional approval it sought in this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents of the pipeline and normal permitting process

for.name: Sen. John Hoeven
for.what_they_did: Introduced and sponsored the bill to approve the Keystone XL pipeline by statute.

for.name: 11 Senate Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including senators from oil- and gas-producing and pipeline-route states.

for.name: 45 of 45 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Every Republican voting voted yes on the bill.

for.name: Sen. Mary Landrieu
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill and publicly pressed for a Senate vote on Keystone XL before her December 2014 runoff election.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Kept Keystone XL approval bills off the Senate floor through most of the 113th Congress; the bill only reached the floor by unanimous consent under a late-2014 agreement.

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Kept the pipeline decision in the slow State Department permitting review and signaled he would not approve it, pressuring senators ahead of the vote.

against.name: Environmental and climate groups
against.what_they_did: Ran public campaigns against Keystone XL approval, citing spill risk over the Ogallala aquifer and the climate impact of tar sands oil.

sides.party_line_note: The vote was nearly unanimous on each side of the aisle: all 45 Republicans voted yes, 39 of 53 Democrats voted no, 14 Democrats broke ranks to vote yes, and both independents voted no.

industries.note: The bill would have handed one company direct congressional approval of its pipeline, bypassing the remaining environmental review and the usual court challenges. Its gain comes at the cost of the public's normal review and recourse rights.
A new pipeline to Gulf Coast refineries would expand the market for tar sands crude. Producers benefit from the route; the public bears the spill and climate risks.
Construction firms would gain a large multi-state project and the temporary jobs that come with it, which is the main benefit supporters cited for workers.

industries.industry: Railroads hauling crude by tank car
industries.note: Railroads currently move much of the region's crude; a pipeline would take some of that business. The shift away from tank-car shipments would also reduce a major spill-and-safety hazard for towns along rail lines.
